title: Choir and Winter
premise: Kestrel Oyelaran hosts a small-town overnight radio show, 'The Quiet Hours,' where callers sometimes turn out to be the recently dead—people who died within the week, calling in to finish unfinished business. Kestrel has inherited the show, the station building, and a set of rules from their grandmother: keep the lights on, count the doors, never answer the second voice. When new sleep-recording equipment captures something in the studio answering questions Kestrel never asked aloud, they learn their grandmother didn't run the show to help ghosts—she ran it as bait and boundary, feeding the thing below the station just enough attention to keep it asleep. As the entity wakes and begins wearing the voices of everyone Kestrel has ever lost, including their grandmother, Kestrel must decide whether to break the inheritance entirely by going silent on air forever, or take up the microphone one last time at dawn. In the climax, Kestrel answers the second voice directly, claiming the inheritance on their own terms—not as prey or priest but as equal—and the entity, denied both fear and worship, recedes back beneath the floorboards. The book ends with sunrise, an empty chair at the broadcast desk, and Kestrel walking away from the station as it quietly forgets them.
about_author: Xanthe Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years working the graveyard shift at a station built over something older than the town itself. They write horror about inheritances—the houses, habits, and hauntings we receive whether we asked for them or not.

chapters.title: Sign-Off at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. We meet the station, the rules (lights on, doors counted), and the format of 'The Quiet Hours.' A caller named Marisol talks to her dead brother; Kestrel recognizes the signs of a week-old voice and handles it gently. Emotional beat: weary competence masking loneliness—we see Kestrel is good at this and hates that they're good at this.

chapters.title: The Inheritance Clause
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, flashback woven through present-day inventory of the station. Grandmother Odile's will left Kestrel everything: the building, the transmitter, a locked tape archive, and a handwritten rulebook with one page torn out. Emotional beat: resentment curdling into curiosity—Kestrel resents being chosen but can't stop reading.

chapters.title: Caller Unknown
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A caller claims to be Danny Fitch, who died Tuesday; his widow calls minutes later confirming details no one else knew. Kestrel follows procedure, gives him airtime, lets him say goodbye. But afterward the board lights stay lit for eleven seconds with no caller connected. Emotional beat: dread arriving politely, like a guest who knows your name.

chapters.title: The Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Installing donated sleep-monitoring equipment for a segment on insomnia, Kestrel records themselves napping in the studio's back room. Playback captures a second voice answering questions Kestrel murmured in sleep—questions about the torn-out page. Emotional beat: violation; the most private self has been in conversation without consent.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, consulting the rulebook and the locked archive. Rules surface piecemeal: never answer the second voice, never broadcast after 5:59, never let it learn your birth name. The torn page's stub reads only '...and if it asks you what you are.' Emotional beat: the horror of incomplete instructions—an inheritance that assumes knowledge Kestrel doesn't have.

chapters.title: What Marisol Heard
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Marisol, the grieving sister from chapter one, calls again—this time her dead brother answers on the first ring before she speaks, using words she hadn't said yet. She begs Kestrel to explain. Kestrel lies badly. Emotional beat: guilt; Kestrel realizes the show isn't a service, it's exposure—and listeners are catching whatever the station catches.

chapters.title: Doors
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The door count comes up wrong: thirteen doors in a twelve-door building. Kestrel walks the halls at 4 a.m., counting aloud, while something behind each door counts along in a different voice—each one someone Kestrel has buried or broadcast. Emotional beat: claustrophobic terror; home becomes a throat.

chapters.title: Odile's Last Tape
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, listening to a reel from the archive dated the night before Odile's death. Odile speaks to the second voice casually, almost fondly, negotiating—then addresses the future listener directly: 'Whoever's hearing this, it already knows your name. It learned mine the same way.' Emotional beat: grief weaponized; the grandmother's voice becomes both comfort and warning.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Gets a Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. During a live broadcast, the second voice slips onto the open mic and answers a listener's question before Kestrel can—correctly, kindly, devastatingly. Callers love it. Ratings spike. Management wants more. Emotional beat: seduction; the horror discovers it can be popular, and popularity is a kind of permission.

chapters.title: Dead Air Discipline
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, fighting the station's new enthusiasm. Kestrel tries silence protocols, cutting mics, pre-taped shows. Every workaround fails differently; the voice adapts, appearing in the tape hiss, in the sponsor copy, in Kestrel's own recorded promos. Emotional beat: erosion—control slipping one reasonable compromise at a time.

chapters.title: It Knows My Middle Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The voice uses Kestrel's full birth name on air—a name Kestrel changed years ago and told no one at the station. Identity theme sharpens: the entity doesn't haunt bodies, it haunts names, and it's offering Kestrel an older name still, one from before Oyelaran. Emotional beat: vertigo of selfhood; being known completely feels indistinguishable from being owned.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, breaking into the archive's sealed cabinet. The missing page, hidden inside a dead console, completes the sentence: '...and if it asks you what you are, do not answer honestly, because honest things can be eaten.' Kestrel understands the trap they've been sleeping inside. Emotional beat: cold clarity—the rules weren't superstition, they were survival grammar.

chapters.title: Listeners Who Died Last Week
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV chapter: three callers' perspectives interwoven—Marisol, the widow Ruth, and a teenage fan—all drawn back to the frequency at night, all dreaming of a warm room under the studio. Each hears the second voice practicing their loved ones' laughter. Emotional beat: communal dread; the audience is becoming material.

chapters.title: Management Meeting at Midnight
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV with station manager Devraj. He won't kill the ratings golden goose; he suggests giving the voice its own segment. Kestrel refuses; Devraj reveals the station's owners have held the property since 1931 and have always required 'continuous broadcast.' Emotional beat: institutional horror—the corruption isn't supernatural first, it's contractual.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, reconstructing the origin: in 1931 the station's founders broadcast a séance to boost signal strength and invited something to speak through the tower. Every host since has kept it fed with attention. Odile tried to starve it; it killed her gently, in her sleep, mid-broadcast. Emotional beat: furious grief—Kestrel was handed a debt disguised as a legacy.

chapters.title: The Voice Wears Odile
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The second voice stops pretending and arrives as Grandmother Odile, perfect down to the humming, offering to teach Kestrel 'how we really run the show.' For one terrible hour Kestrel talks with her. Then the mask slips mid-sentence and asks, sweetly, what Kestrel is. Kestrel says nothing. Barely. Emotional beat: heartbreak weaponized—the cruelest haunting is the one you want.

chapters.title: Counting Doors at Dawn's Edge
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, the night before the finale. Kestrel prepares: burns nothing, breaks nothing, instead writes their own page for the rulebook. They call every listener and tell them not to tune in tomorrow. Most obey. Marisol doesn't. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into sacrifice—Kestrel chooses to end the show even though the show is the only place they've ever belonged.

chapters.title: Final Broadcast, Part One
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, live. 5:00 a.m. Kestrel goes on air and tells the town the truth: the dead callers were real, the voice is real, and the station has been a mouth. Listeners flood the lines—some screaming, some begging to hear their dead one last time. The second voice rises through every phone line at once. Emotional beat: terrifying liberation; truth as a flare burned in a dark field.

chapters.title: Final Broadcast, Part Two
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The entity drops all masks and asks the question: 'What are you?' Kestrel answers—not honestly, not falsely, but on their own terms: 'I'm the one holding the microphone.' Power reframed: authority isn't inherited, it's seized in the moment of speech. The tower screams static. Emotional beat: climax—defiance as exorcism.

chapters.title: Sunrise Protocol
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At 5:59 Kestrel does what no host has done: signs off permanently, mid-word, and pulls the master breaker while the entity is still speaking through the dead air. The building exhales. Doors recount correctly: twelve. Somewhere below, something settles back to sleep, unfed and unentertained. Emotional beat: exhausted triumph with a tremor underneath.

chapters.title: After the Frequency
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, weeks later. The station sits silent; the town half-remembers a radio show the way you remember a dream. Marisol visits, healed enough to bring coffee instead of questions. Kestrel finds the rulebook and adds their own final line: 'When you leave, mean it.' Emotional beat: quiet mourning for the strange gift of the show.

chapters.title: Someone Else's Quiet Hours
chapters.summary: Distant third-person epilogue. A new owner tours the shuttered station, delighted by the vintage equipment, the old tapes, the handwritten rules tucked in a drawer. That night, testing the console alone, they hear the board light up—no caller connected—for exactly eleven seconds. Final image: a hand reaching, almost idly, for the ON AIR switch. Emotional beat: cyclical chill; inheritance always finds a next of kin.
